newsitem.title: SPAIN: No record of "Operation Mengele" -- Spanish spies.
newsitem.headline: No record of "Operation Mengele" -- Spanish spies.

text.p: Spain's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday it had no record of vagrants being kidnapped and used as guinea pigs for anti-guerrilla drugs, but stopped short of an outright denial of this so-called "Operation Mengele".

After withholding comment all day on Tuesday, the ministry said in a statement that the military intelligence agency CESID had no documentary evidence of the operation but disclosed that Spain's best-known judge, Baltasar Garzon, had been probing the affair since early August.

The daily El Mundo, quoting military intelligence files and agents, said on Tuesday the 1988 experiments in which a beggar died had been given their gruesome nickname within the service because of Nazi death-camp doctor Josef Mengele.

The anaesthetic drugs tested on vagrants were meant to help security forces kidnap guerrillas of the separatist organisation ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) from hideaways in southern France and smuggle them back to Spain, El Mundo said.

The Defence Ministry's assertion that there is no documentary evidence could refer to charges that a disgruntled former head of covert operations at CESID walked out with thousands of compromising top-secret files.

Colonel Juan Alberto Perote is under detention and on trial for stealing these papers. He is one of the key witnesses in cases against members of the former Socialist government for a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque rebels.

Officials say that Perote eventually returned the files -- but in the form of legally worthless copies rather than the originals. Fingers are often pointed at the colonel when a fresh compromising facsimile appears in the local press.
El Mundo reproduced on its front page on Wednesday a copy of what it said was the CESID's official cover form for the entire operation, including classification details and case officers.

The Defence Ministry said Judge Garzon's inquiries had been answered with an official note stating: "There is in that centre (CESID) no document, element or data relating to any tests or experiments that may have been carried out with vagrants or drug addicts who were kidnapped and taken to CESID premises."

The ministry said the use of the affirmative past tense "were", which might imply that the kidnaps at least did take place, had been used only because its lawyers had copied the phrasing of Garzon's question in their reply.

General Emilio Alonso Manglano, who led the CESID for 14 years until June 1995, declined to answer reporters' questions when he appeared in court on Tuesday over the bugging by his service of the mobile telephones of prominent Spaniards including King Juan Carlos -- a scandal which cost him his job.
Manglano is also being indicted over the kidnapping, torture and murder of two presumed Basque separatist guerrillas in 1983.
The "dirty war" of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder against presumed ETA members killed 27 people between 1983 and 1987, mostly in southern France. A third were killed by mistake.

Former Socialist interior minister Jose Barrionuevo and Enrique Rodriguez Galindo, a top general in the paramilitary Civil Guard, are on trial on charges of creating and running the death squads that waged the illegal campaign.
